stem: The graph of f near x = 1 has these features: as x approaches 1 from the left, y approaches 2; as x approaches 1 from the right, y approaches 5; and f(1) = 3. The graph of g near x = 1 has these features: as x approaches 1 from the left, y approaches 3; as x approaches 1 from the right, y approaches 0; and g(1) = 4. Which of the following is true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: lim(x→1) [f(x) + g(x)] exists and equals 5, but lim(x→1) [f(x)·g(x)] does not exist.
choices.rationale: Correct: Left side: sum 2 + 3 = 5, product 2·3 = 6. Right side: sum 5 + 0 = 5, product 5·0 = 0. The sum has equal one-sided limits 5; the product has 6 and 0.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neither lim(x→1) [f(x) + g(x)] nor lim(x→1) [f(x)·g(x)] exists, because neither f nor g has a limit at x = 1.
choices.rationale: A sum can have a limit even when each term has none; here the one-sided sums are 2 + 3 = 5 from the left and 5 + 0 = 5 from the right, so the sum does have a limit.

choices.label: C
choices.text: lim(x→1) [f(x)·g(x)] exists and equals 0, but lim(x→1) [f(x) + g(x)] does not exist.
choices.rationale: The one-sided product limits are 2·3 = 6 from the left and 5·0 = 0 from the right, which disagree, so the product has no limit; 0 is only the right-hand value.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both limits exist: lim(x→1) [f(x) + g(x)] = 7 and lim(x→1) [f(x)·g(x)] = 12.
choices.rationale: Adding and multiplying f(1) = 3 and g(1) = 4 uses function values, but a limit depends only on the behavior near x = 1, not on the value at 1.

stem: The graph of f near x = 2 has these features: from the left, y approaches 4; from the right, y approaches −1; and f(2) = 1. The graph of g near x = 2: from the left, y approaches −2; from the right, y approaches 3; and g(2) = 0. Which of the following is true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: lim(x→2) [f(x) + g(x)] exists and equals 2, but lim(x→2) [f(x) − g(x)] does not exist.
choices.rationale: Correct: Left: f + g → 4 + (−2) = 2 and f − g → 4 − (−2) = 6. Right: f + g → −1 + 3 = 2 and f − g → −1 − 3 = −4. The sum agrees (2) and the difference does not (6 versus −4).

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both limits exist: lim(x→2) [f(x) + g(x)] = 1 and lim(x→2) [f(x) − g(x)] = 1.
choices.rationale: This substitutes f(2) = 1 and g(2) = 0, but a limit is determined by nearby values, not by the value at the point.

choices.label: C
choices.text: lim(x→2) [f(x) − g(x)] exists and equals 6, but lim(x→2) [f(x) + g(x)] does not exist.
choices.rationale: The value 6 is only the left-hand limit of the difference; the right-hand limit is −1 − 3 = −4, so the difference has no limit, while the sum, whose one-sided limits are both 2, does.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither limit exists, because f and g do not have limits at x = 2.
choices.rationale: Individual limits failing to exist does not prevent a combination from having one; the left and right sums are both 2.

choices.label: B

stem: A table lists values of f(x) = sin(π/x) at x = 1/2, 1/4, 1/10, 1/100, and 1/1000, and also at the negatives of these numbers. Every value in the table is 0. A student writes, "lim(x→0) f(x) = 0, because the table values are all 0." Which statement best evaluates the student's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The conclusion is correct: ten different inputs close to 0 on both sides all give 0, so the limit is 0.
choices.rationale: A finite list of values, even on both sides of 0, cannot prove a limit; the tabulated inputs all happen to be of the form 1/n where the sine is 0, and other inputs give other values.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The conclusion is incorrect: the limit is +∞, because π/x grows without bound as x approaches 0.
choices.rationale: The argument π/x does grow without bound, but sin of an unbounded argument keeps oscillating between −1 and 1 rather than growing, so the limit is not +∞.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The conclusion is incorrect: the limit is 1, because f reaches its maximum value 1 arbitrarily close to 0.
choices.rationale: The function takes the value 1 near 0 but also takes the values 0 and −1 near 0, so it does not settle at 1; a limit requires f to approach a single number.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The conclusion is incorrect: the limit does not exist, because f(x) = 1 at x = 2/5, 2/9, 2/13, ..., which also approach 0.
choices.rationale: Correct: sin(π/x) = 0 at x = 1/n, but at x = 2/(4k + 1) it equals sin((4k + 1)π/2) = 1; two sequences approaching 0 give different values (0 and 1), so no limit.

stem: A student tabulates g(x) = cos(π/x) at x = 1/2, 1/4, 1/6, 1/8, and 1/100, finds g(x) = 1 every time, and concludes that lim(x→0+) g(x) = 1. Which statement is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The conclusion is correct: the values equal 1 at inputs that get arbitrarily close to 0 from the right.
choices.rationale: All five inputs are even reciprocals 1/(2n), where cos(2nπ) = 1; a sample on one special sequence does not decide the limit, and inputs 1/(2n + 1) give −1.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The conclusion is incorrect: the limit is 0, because cos oscillates between −1 and 1 and the values average out to 0.
choices.rationale: Averaging the extreme values is not how limits work; a limit exists only if g approaches one number, and g keeps hitting both 1 and −1 near 0.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The conclusion is incorrect: the limit is −1, because g(1/3) = −1 shows the true value that the table missed.
choices.rationale: The value −1 on odd reciprocals is equally unrepresentative as the value 1 on even reciprocals; neither one is the limit.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The conclusion is incorrect: the limit does not exist, because g(x) = −1 at x = 1/3, 1/5, 1/7, ..., which also approach 0 from the right.
choices.rationale: Correct: cos(π/x) at x = 1/(2n) is cos(2nπ) = 1, and at x = 1/(2n + 1) is cos((2n + 1)π) = −1. Two sequences approaching 0+ give 1 and −1, so the limit does not exist.

stem: A table lists values of h(x) = x·sin(π/x) at x = 1/2, 1/4, 1/10, 1/100, and 1/1000, and every value is 0. A student claims lim(x→0) h(x) = 0. Which statement gives the best justification that this claim is true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The table shows h(x) = 0 at five inputs approaching 0, so the limit is 0.
choices.rationale: The claim happens to be true, but the table cannot justify it because the sampled inputs all make sin(π/x) = 0; a bound valid for all x near 0 is needed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Since sin(π/x) has no limit at 0, the product x·sin(π/x) has no limit at 0 either.
choices.rationale: A product can have a limit even if one factor does not; here the factor x → 0 squeezes the bounded oscillation to 0.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Since −|x| ≤ x·sin(π/x) ≤ |x| for x ≠ 0 and both bounds approach 0, the Squeeze Theorem gives lim(x→0) h(x) = 0.
choices.rationale: Correct: |x·sin(π/x)| ≤ |x| and |x| → 0, so the Squeeze Theorem gives 0. The table is only suggestive because sin(π/x) = 0 at every 1/n.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Since sin(π/x) oscillates between −1 and 1, the limit is the average of these, which is 0, regardless of the factor x.
choices.rationale: The limit is 0 because the factor x forces the amplitude to 0, not because the oscillation averages out; without the factor x the oscillation would give no limit.

title: classify a discontinuity from one-sided limits of an inverse-trigonometric expression and reject an argument that confus
stem: Let f(x) = arctan(1/(x − 2)) for x ≠ 2, and let f(2) = 0. A student argues, "f has a removable discontinuity at x = 2, because the one-sided limits are −π/2 and π/2, which average to f(2) = 0." Which statement is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The discontinuity is a jump: the one-sided limits are −π/2 and π/2, so the jump has size π.
choices.rationale: Correct: As x → 2−, 1/(x − 2) → −∞ and arctan → −π/2. As x → 2+, arctan → π/2. The one-sided limits are finite and unequal, so this is a jump of π/2 − (−π/2) = π.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The student is correct: the discontinuity is removable.
choices.rationale: A removable discontinuity requires the two-sided limit to exist, and here the one-sided limits differ; f(2) being their average does not make the limit exist.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The discontinuity is infinite, because 1/(x − 2) is unbounded near x = 2.
choices.rationale: The inner expression is unbounded, but arctan is bounded, so f itself stays between −π/2 and π/2 and the one-sided limits are finite, which excludes an infinite discontinuity.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The discontinuity is a jump of size π/2, which is the distance from f(2) = 0 to either one-sided limit.
choices.rationale: The size of a jump is the difference between the two one-sided limits, π/2 − (−π/2) = π, not the distance from f(2) to one side.

stem: Let g(x) = 1/(1 + e^(1/(x − 1))) for x ≠ 1, and let g(1) = 1/2. Which statement correctly describes g at x = 1?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is a removable discontinuity, because g(1) = 1/2 lies halfway between the one-sided limits.
choices.rationale: Removable requires lim g to exist; the one-sided limits are 1 and 0, so no two-sided limit exists, regardless of where g(1) is placed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is an infinite discontinuity, because the exponent 1/(x − 1) is unbounded near 1.
choices.rationale: The exponent is unbounded, but g itself is squeezed between 0 and 1 near x = 1, so its one-sided limits are finite and the discontinuity is not infinite.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a jump discontinuity, of size 1.
choices.rationale: Correct: As x → 1+, the exponent → +∞, e^(…) → ∞, so g → 0. As x → 1−, the exponent → −∞, e^(…) → 0, so g → 1. Finite, unequal one-sided limits 1 and 0 give a jump of size 1.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a jump discontinuity, of size 1/2.
choices.rationale: The jump size is the difference of the one-sided limits, 1 − 0 = 1; the value 1/2 is only the defined value g(1).

stem: Let h(x) = e^(1/(x + 1)) for x ≠ −1. Which statement correctly describes the discontinuity of h at x = −1?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is removable, because lim(x→−1−) h(x) = 0 exists.

choices.rationale: A jump requires both one-sided limits to be finite numbers; here the right-hand one is +∞, which makes it an infinite discontinuity.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is oscillating, because the exponent 1/(x + 1) changes sign at x = −1.
choices.rationale: The exponent changes sign but the function does not oscillate; it tends monotonically to 0 on one side and grows without bound on the other.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is infinite, because lim(x→−1+) h(x) = +∞.
choices.rationale: Correct: As x → −1−, the exponent → −∞ so h → 0. As x → −1+, the exponent → +∞ so h → +∞. One side is unbounded, so the discontinuity is infinite.

title: classify a discontinuity from one-sided limits of an inverse-trigonometric expression and reject an argument that confus (variant 3)
stem: Let g(x) = arctan(1/(x − 3)²) for x ≠ 3, and let g(3) = 0. Which statement correctly describes g at x = 3?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is an infinite discontinuity, because 1/(x − 3)² is unbounded near 3.
choices.rationale: The inside expression is unbounded, but arctan is bounded, so g stays below π/2 and approaches π/2 from both sides; the limit is finite, which rules out an infinite discontinuity.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a removable discontinuity, because lim(x→3) g(x) = π/2 exists but is not equal to g(3).
choices.rationale: Correct: As x → 3 from either side, 1/(x − 3)² → +∞ and arctan → π/2. So lim g = π/2, while g(3) = 0 ≠ π/2.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a jump of size π/2, the difference between g(3) = 0 and the value π/2 near 3.
choices.rationale: Both one-sided limits equal π/2, so there is no jump between the left and right sides; the mismatch is only with the defined value g(3).

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is not a discontinuity, because g(3) = 0 is a finite number.
choices.rationale: Continuity requires g(3) to equal the limit π/2, and being finite is not enough; since g(3) = 0 ≠ π/2, g is discontinuous.
